title: SPA/342/2018 of Dr. Priyanka Arora AND OTHERS Vs Himanshu Joshi AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Special Appeal No. 342 of 2018
Dr. Priyanka Arora and others. ........ Appellants
Versus
Himanshu Joshi and others. .......Respondents

Mr. Pankaj Kumar Along with Mr. Harendra Belwal, Advocate for the appellants.
Mr. Vinay Kumar, Advocate for respondent nos. 1 to 7 / writ petitioners.
Mr. Paresh Tripathi, Chief Standing Counsel for the State of Uttarakhand / respondent
nos. 8 & 9.
Mr. Alok Mahra & Mr. Bhagwat Mahra, Advocate for the interveners.
Coram: Hon'ble K.M. Joseph, C.J.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
Dated: 20th July, 2018
K.M. Joseph, C.J. (Oral)
 Application (CLMA No. 6 of 2018) for leave to
Appeal is allowed and the leave is granted.
2. Appellants, 22 in number, were the interveners before
the learned Single Judge. Respondent Nos. 1 to 7 in the
Appeal/writ petitioners had approached the learned Single Judge
seeking the following reliefs:
"I. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Mandamus declaring the Uttarakhand Regularization of
Services of Employees appointed as Daily Wager,
Workcharged, Consolidated, Part-time and Adhoc
(Amended) Rules, 2016 as illegal, arbitrary,
unconstitutional and ultra vires to Article 14 & 16 of the
Constitution of India and also against the mandate of the
Constitutional Bench judgment of the Hon'ble Apex
Court in the case of Uma Devi.
II. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Mandamus restraining the respondent State Government
from undertaking any exercise for regularising the
services of Daily Wager, Warkcharged, Consolidated,
Part-time employees working on contract basis or
through outsourcing agencies on substantive vacancies of

2
the department, in terms of the provisions of Amended
Reguarization Rules of 2016.
III. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Certiorari quashing the Government Order dated
19.12.2006 and Govt. Order dated 27.12.2016 issued by
the Secretary, Personnel, Government of Uttarakhand
being illegal, arbitrary, irrational and against the Policy
of Public Employment in State services as guaranteed
under Article 14 & 16 of the Constitution of India.
IV. Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Mandamus commanding and directing the respondent
State Government to treat vacancies of direct recruitment
against which the contractual/daily wager/workcharged
/part-time/adhoc employees are working as substantive
vacancies and to supply these substantive vacancies in
different departments of the State by initiating regular
selection process as pr the mandate of Article 14 & 16 of
the Constitution of India."
3. In brief, the case of the writ petitioners before the
learned Single Judge was as follows:
 They are eligible and competent to apply for the
vacancies arising under the Public Services of the State and have
been submitting their application forms against the advertisement
issued by the Examining Body from time to time for appointment
on group 'C' posts in different departments of the State. It is their
case that the effect of the impugned Amended Regularization
Rules-2016, was that the petitioners were deprived of their rights
to be considered for public employment, due to regularization
their avenues of selection are being affected. They laid store by
the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of
Secretary, State of Karnataka and Ors. Vs. Uma Devi and
others reported in (2006) 4 SCC 1. They pointed out the earlier
Rules, which have been framed for the first time in the year 2011
in the State of Uttarakhand, also provided for regularisation. This
was followed up by the Rules of 2013, which again tended to
continue with the practice of regularization, and finally, came the

3
amendment of the year 2016, by which the unconstitutional
practice of regularisation was sought to be perpetuated. This
argument of the learned counsel for the writ petitioners found
favour with the learned Single Judge. In the judgment, which is
impugned, the learned Single Judge interfered with the
impugned amendment of the year 2016, held it to be violative of
Article 14 and being in clear violation of Uma Devi's judgment
and quashed the amendment of 2016.
4. Appellants/interveners before the learned Single
Judge claimed that they are working as Ayurvedic Medical
Officers. It is their case, inter alia, that they were appointed in
the year 2010. It is their further case that they underwent a
selection process, which followed an advertisement inviting
applications from the qualified hands. It is also their case that the
selection was undertaken after following the reservation policy.
There is no dispute that actually under the Rules, the procedure of
selection for making regular appointments contemplates
consultation with the Public Service Commission. In other
words, on reporting vacancies, the Public Service Commission is
obliged to hold regular selection and to prepare a proper select
list, which has not been done in the case of the appellants and it is
not in dispute, but according to them, but for that, a selection
procedure has been undergone as aforesaid observing the
principle of reservation. There is a case that the appellants are all
qualified and there were vacancies available. The appellants were
appointed on contractual basis. In the order of appointment of the
appellants, undoubtedly, it is recited that they will continue till
the regular hands join.
5. The appellants take exception to paragraphs 24 and
26 of the judgment, which read as follows:
"24. However, it is made clear that for all such posts on
which the regularization was being made pursuant to
the amendment of 2016 though the Government cannot

4
regularize the ad hoc, temporary or contractual
employees on these posts but these posts cannot remain
vacant as well, therefore, Government shall take
immediate steps for filling up these vacancies in
accordance with law and as per the prescribed selection
procedure, but since some of the candidates might be
working on these sanctioned posts for the last many
years, the Government would always be at liberty to
grant a reasonable "weightage point" and "age
relaxation" to such candidates, in making regular
selection on those posts by making these posts
available by way of an open competition.
26. A reference here of three intervention applications
filed on behalf of those who were appointed as Staff
Nurse and Lab Technician in a newly constituted State
medical college in District Pauri Garhwal known as
"Veer Chandra Singh Garhwali Government Medical
Science and Research Institute, Srinagar", needs
mention (In Application CLMA Nos. 8448 of 2017,
2273 of 2017 & 4713 of 2018). Their case is somewhat
different. Admittedly, the college itself was constituted
in the year 2008 and on 25.2.2009 the posts of Lab
Technician and Staff Nurse were created by the State
Government in the said newly constituted college and
thereafter on 28.2.2009, an advertisement was issued
by the State Government inviting applications from
eligible candidates for filling up these posts against
which the interveners applied and were appointed. Yet
their appointment was not a regular appointment and it
was called a "contractual appointment", for the reason
that till that time (and even now), no rules were framed
for recruitment of Staff Nurse and Lab Technician in
the said medical college. Therefore, in these peculiar
facts and circumstances where there was an urgent
need for manning the medical college by Staff Nurses
and Lab Technicians, and there being no other option,
such a measure was adopted. As there was no service
rules, and in any case, the Government could have
resorted later a one-time measure for regularization,
this case is distinguished from the rest."
6. We heard Mr. Pankaj Kumar along with Mr.
Harendra Belwal, learned counsel for the appellants and Mr.
Vinay Kumar, learned counsel who appears on behalf of the writ
petitioners. We also heard Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief
Standing Counsel for the State of Uttarakhand, besides hearing

5
Mr. Alok Mahra and Mr. Bhagwat Mehra, Advocates, who
appeared for the interveners in the writ petition, whose cause is
dealt with in paragraph 26.
7. Mr. Pankaj Kumar, learned counsel for the appellants
would point out that while the appellants do not take exception to
interference by the learned Single Judge with the amended Rules,
they complain about what is stated in Paragraph No. 24 of the
judgment. He would submit that the appellants were also in line
for regularisation and almost all the persons, who were working
earlier derived the benefit of regularisation and stand regularized
in same capacity, but they have been denied. He would submit
that the appointment of the appellants cannot be described as
illegal; this is for the reasons that there were vacancies arising out
on regular posts; they possess the requisite qualifications; an
open selection procedure was undergone, which involved calling
for applications; and the reservation policy was observed.
Therefore, this cannot be treated as a case, where the selection is
illegal. The only thing that remained to be done was that the
intervention of the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission was
not obtained. In fact, he would submit that the appellants are only
22 in number, though there are 218 vacancies and we are
concerned with the case of Ayurvedic Medical Practitioners in
this case. He would draw our attention to a large body of case
law. He would submit that it is true that interpreting the judgment
of the Hon'ble Apex Court in Uma Devi (supra), the Hon'ble
Apex Court has, no doubt, in the case of State of Karnataka and
Others Vs. M.L. Kesari and others reported in (2010) 9 SCC
247 held, inter alia, as follows:
"5. The decision in State of Karnataka v. Umadevi was
rendered on 10.4.2006. In that case, a Constitution Bench
of this Court held that appointments made without
following the due process or the rules relating to

6
appointment did not confer any right on the appointees
and courts cannot direct their absorption, regularization
or re- engagement nor make their service permanent, and
the High Court in exercise of jurisdiction under Article
226 of the Constitution should not ordinarily issue
directions for absorption, regularization, or permanent
continuance unless the recruitment had been done in a
regular manner, in terms of the constitutional scheme;
and that the courts must be careful in ensuring that they
do not interfere unduly with the economic arrangement
of its affairs by the State or its instrumentalities, nor lend
themselves to be instruments to facilitate the bypassing
of the constitutional and statutory mandates.
6. This Court in Umadevi further held that a temporary,
contractual, casual or a daily-wage employee does not
have a legal right to be made permanent unless he had
been appointed in terms of the relevant rules or in
adherence of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. This
Court however made one exception to the above position
and the same is extracted below : (scc p.42, para 53)
"53. One aspect needs to be clarified. There may
be cases where irregular appointments (not
illegal appointments) as explained in S.V.
Narayanappa [1967 (1) SCR 128], R.N.
Nanjundappa [1972 (1) SCC 409] and B.N.
Nagarajan [1979 (4) SCC 507] and referred to in
para 15 above, of duly qualified persons in duly
sanctioned vacant posts might have been made
and the employees have continued to work for
ten years or more but without the intervention of
orders of the courts or of tribunals. The question
of regularization of the services of such
employees may have to be considered on merits
in the light of the principles settled by this Court
in the cases above referred to and in the light of
this judgment. In that context, the Union of India,
the State Governments and their instrumentalities
should take steps to regularize as a one-time
measure, the services of such irregularly
appointed, who have worked for ten years or
more in duly sanctioned posts but not under
cover of orders of the courts or of tribunals and
should further ensure that regular recruitments
are undertaken to fill those vacant sanctioned
posts that require to be filled up, in cases where
temporary employees or daily wagers are being
now employed. The process must be set in
motion within six months from this date. ...."
(emphasis in original)

7
7. It is evident from the above that there is an exception
to the general principles against `regularization'
enunciated in Umadevi, if the following conditions are
fulfilled :
(i) The employee concerned should have worked
for 10 years or more in duly sanctioned post
without the benefit or protection of the interim
order of any court or tribunal. In other words, the
State Government or its instrumentality should
have employed the employee and continued him
in service voluntarily and continuously for more
than ten years.
(ii) The appointment of such employee should
not be illegal, even if irregular. Where the
appointments are not made or continued against
sanctioned posts or where the persons appointed
do not possess the prescribed minimum
qualifications, the appointments will be
considered to be illegal. But where the person
employed possessed the prescribed qualifications
and was working against sanctioned posts, but
had been selected without undergoing the process
of open competitive selection, such appointments
are considered to be irregular."
 But, we may also notice Paragraph No. 11 of the said
judgment, which reads as follows:
"11. The object behind the said direction in para 53 of
Umadevi is two- fold. First is to ensure that those who
have put in more than ten years of continuous service
without the protection of any interim orders of courts or
tribunals, before the date of decision in Umadevi was
rendered, are considered for regularization in view of
their long service. Second is to ensure that the
departments/instrumentalities do not perpetuate the
practice of employing persons on daily-wage/ad-hoc/casual basis for long periods and then periodically
regularize them on the ground that they have served for
more than ten years, thereby defeating the constitutional
or statutory provisions relating to recruitment and
appointment. The true effect of the direction is that all
persons who have worked for more than ten years as on
10.4.2006 (the date of decision in Umadevi) without the
protection of any interim order of any court or tribunal, in
vacant posts, possessing the requisite qualification, are
entitled to be considered for regularization. The fact that
the employer has not undertaken such exercise of

8
regularization within six months of the decision in
Umadevi or that such exercise was undertaken only in
regard to a limited few, will not disentitle such
employees, the right to be considered for regularization
in terms of the above directions in Umadevi as a one-time measure."

8. He, undoubtedly, sought to derive considerable support
from the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Nihal
Singh and others vs. State of Punjab and others reported in (2013)
14 SCC Page 65. In the said case, undoubtedly, the Hon'ble Apex
Court held in favour of the appellants / writ petitioners and directed
regularization of service of the appellants as Special Police Officers,
who undoubtedly, were appointed in the wake of the turbulent
situation prevailing in the State of Punjab decades ago. He would
further submit that the appellants apprehend immediate termination of
their services following the directions contained in Paragraph 24 of
the judgment under challenge in Appeal. He would submit that it is,
at any rate, not necessary to dispense with the services of the
appellants in the light of Paragraph 24 of the judgment.
9. Mr. Pankaj Kumar, learned counsel for the appellants
would also draw our attention to Paragraph 43 of the judgment of the
Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Uma Devi (supra), which reads as
under:
"43. Thus, it is clear that adherence to the rule of
equality in public employment is a basic feature of our
Constitution and since the rule of law is the core of our
Constitution, a Court would certainly be disabled from
passing an order upholding a violation of Article 14 or in
ordering the overlooking of the need to comply with the
requirements of Article 14 read with Article 16 of the
Constitution. Therefore, consistent with the scheme for
public employment, this Court while laying down the
law, has necessarily to hold that unless the appointment
is in terms of the relevant rules and after a proper
competition among qualified persons, the same would
not confer any right on the appointee. If it is a contractual
appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end
of the contract, if it were an engagement or appointment
on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to
an end when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary

9
employee could not claim to be made permanent on the
expiry of his term of appointment. It has also to be
clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a
casual wage worker is continued for a time beyond the
term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be
absorbed in regular service or made permanent, merely
on the strength of such continuance, if the original
appointment was not made by following a due process of
selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open
to the court to prevent regular recruitment at the instance
of temporary employees whose period of employment
has come to an end or of ad hoc employees who by the
very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any
right. The High Courts acting under Article 226 of the
Constitution, should not ordinarily issue directions for
absorption, regularization, or permanent continuance
unless the recruitment itself was made regularly and in
terms of the constitutional scheme. Merely because, an
employee had continued under cover of an order of
Court, which we have described as 'litigious employment'
in the earlier part of the judgment, he would not be
entitled to any right to be absorbed or made permanent in
the service. In fact, in such cases, the High Court may not
be justified in issuing interim directions, since, after all,
if ultimately the employee approaching it is found
entitled to relief, it may be possible for it to mould the
relief in such a manner that ultimately no prejudice will
be caused to him, whereas an interim direction to
continue his employment would hold up the regular
procedure for selection or impose on the State the burden
of paying an employee who is really not required. The
courts must be careful in ensuring that they do not
interfere unduly with the economic arrangement of its
affairs by the State or its instrumentalities or lend
themselves the instruments to facilitate the bypassing of
the constitutional and statutory mandates."
10. Mr. Pankaj Kumar, learned counsel for the appellants
further submitted that the learned Single Judge has granted relief in
Paragraph 26 to the persons covered by the said paragraph. He would
submit that there is no basis for treating the appellants on a different
basis.
11. Mr. Vinay Kumar, learned counsel for the writ
petitioners would, in fact, support the appellants in their submissions
in regard to Paragraph 26. He would also oppose the relief sought that

10
the appellants may be permitted to continue. He would submit that
there is inordinate delay by the Authorities in carrying out regular
recruitment as per law and if any direction is given permitting the
appellants to continue, this will again result in regular selections
getting delayed.
12. Mr. Alok Mahra and Mr. Bhagwat Mehra, who appear
for the interveners, whose case has been discussed in Paragraph No.
26 of the judgment, would point out that their case stands on a
different footing. It is submitted that the Government Medical
College was started in the year 2008; there were no service rules; an
advertisement was issued in the national newspaper; the interveners,
whom they represent, fulfilled the requirements and on the basis of the
selection held by duly constituted Selection Committee, their selection
was made. It is their further case that in their case communal rotation
and reservation was followed. It is their case that it is the absence of
any Rules, which has led to their being kept in the state, in which they
find themselves. It is also pointed out by Shri Alook Mehra that his
clients, in fact, have not been impleaded in the Appeal and they are
making submissions on the basis of a caveat.
13. Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned Chief Standing counsel on
being asked on the submission of the learned counsel for the
appellants regarding the relief, which is claimed that at least the
appellants may not actually be disturbed till the list of the Uttarakhand
Public Service hands is prepared, he submitted that a proposal for
extension of the period of 34 Ayurvedic Medical Officers (which
includes the appellants) and one Unani Medical Officer for
continuation till the regular appointment is made by the Uttarakhand
Public Service Commission has been forwarded to the State
Government and the same is pending consideration. This submission
is based on written instructions dated 20th July, 2018, copy of which
has been handed over to us.
14. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, we are
inclined to clarify what is stated in Paragraph 24 of the impugned

11
judgment. There can be no doubt that the appointment of the
appellants is on contractual basis. The term in the appointment order
makes it abundantly clear that they will have to make way for the
regular recruits. 'Regular recruits' means the persons, who are
selected by the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission. The only
question is, whether in the wake of the directions in Paragraph 24, it
should be axiomatically understood as a peremptory direction to
dislodge the appellants. We notice that the appellants are working as
Ayurvedic Medical Officers since 2010. There is also a case for the
appellants that there are 218 vacancies, but the appellants are 22 in
number. Apparently, there are 12 more going by the figures brought
to our notice by the learned Chief Standing Counsel. Therefore, we
would think that as far as Paragraph 24 is concerned, we need only
make it clear that since the matter is pending consideration before the
Government regarding their continuity, the Government should be left
free to take a decision on it in accordance with law, based on their
contracts and the orders issued from time to time and we need only
clarify that the appellants need not be dislodged only based on the
directions contained in Paragraph 24 of the impugned judgment. At
the same time, we must take care to allay the apprehension of Mr.
Vinay Kumar, learned counsel for the writ petitioner that there is
propensity to delay the regular appointment.
15. As regards the argument addressed with reference to
what is contained in Paragraph 26 of the impugned judgment is
concerned, we do not think that we should give any relief to the
appellants on the said basis. We must notice that, in fact, appellants
are the interveners. The interveners, who are subject matter of
Paragraph 26, also can be treated as the party respondents. It is not as
if the appointment of the interveners can be made subject matter of the
Appeal filed by the appellants. In fact, we notice the submission of
Mr. Alok Mahra that they have not even been made parties to this
Appeal. Further, we do notice that there is some difference between
the appellants and the interveners before the learned Single Judge,
whose case is considered in Paragraph 26. At any rate, in the Appeal

12
filed by the appellants, we do not intend to consider granting any
relief to either them or against the party respondents.
16. Having rendered the above discussion, the upshot of the
same will be as follows:
 The Appeal is disposed of as follows:
 We make it clear that the direction contained in
Paragraph 24 of the impugned judgment need not be understood as a
direction to immediately dislodge the appellants. The Government
will be free to take a decision in this regard as is brought to our notice
by the learned Chief Standing Counsel in accordance with the terms
of the contract, relevant Government Orders and in accordance with
law in regard to the continuity of the appellants. We, however, make
it clear that the process for regular selection must be carried out with
utmost despatch. Learned Chief Standing Counsel would submit in
this regard that the vacancies, namely, 218, which means the
vacancies, which are also occupied by the appellants, have been
reported to the Uttarakhand Public Service Commission, six months
ago; however, certain queries have been posed by the Commission;
they will be answered within a period of two weeks from today
(Uttarakhand Public Service Commission as such is not a party in this
case). Besides recording the submission of the learned Chief Standing
Counsel, we also direct that the queries, which have been posed by the
Commission, will positively be responded to within a period of two
weeks from today by the concerned Authority in the Ayush
Department. On receipt of further information from the concerned
Authority in the Ayush Department, Uttarakhand Public Service
Commission will take follow-up measures and expedite the regular
selection for all 218 posts of Ayurvedic Medical Practitioners,
including the vacancies, which are presently held up by the appellants.
No order as to costs.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma J.) (K.M. Joseph, C.J.)
 20.07.2018
Rathour
